column1: # Player-facing settings: the iOS launcher (dm/ios/Sources/Launcher.swift) and the Mac app's settings window (dm/mac/Launcher.swift) show them before the game starts; Mac front ends read the same list.

# dm/games/settings.py writes one game's list into its app (dm/launcher.json; build_ipa.sh, and dm/mac/pack_app.py through the NSP script): the rows whose condition holds for that game, with its defaults. Each sets an environment variable the host reads when the game starts; one an env file sets
# (Documents/env.txt, the bundle's dm/env.txt) is shown but kept. Diagnostic switches stay environment-only, so they are not listed here. The player's page is docs/settings.md.
#   variable  the environment variable the setting sets

#   kind      choice: values value=label,..., an option only some games have with ?<shown>&<shown> after its label (languages: the game's own, from its control data; every language when it has none, with a note); range: values low:high:step, shown as a percentage;
#             toggle: values - (on sets 1, off 0) or <on>/<off>, the two values the variable takes (on/off)
#   default   a value (a toggle's: 1 on, 0 off); DM_GAME_<NAME>: the host's own default from the game profile (game_profile.h, game.py); build:<VAR>: the IPA build's setting (build_ipa.sh)
#             <ios>|<mac> selects the platform's default before resolving a profile macro or build variable

#   shown     always; DM_GAME_<NAME>!=<value> or ==<value>; fixups:<KEY>: main's rewriter table has that key (a stub in the game's build, patch_nso.py); languages>1 (more than one to pick, so also when the control data lists none); gfxapi:<API>: the packer's GFXAPI;
#             platform:<ios | mac>: the app's platform (SETTINGS_PLATFORM, ios when unset), for a switch only that platform's front end reads
#   section   Game, Controls or Performance: a heading on the single settings screen. Rows appear in table order within each section
#             Reset to tested defaults clears all launcher choices; values fixed by an env file stay
#   label, note  the setting's name and the line under it (may be empty): its cost (latency, memory, heat), then the setting recommended, as "Recommended: ..."
#   meta      optional, key=value pairs separated by ; (settings.py META lists the keys; docs/frontends.md, The settings list, describes them):
#             level=basic  a setting a front end shows first;  needs=<VAR>=<value>  a sub-setting, drawn only while the row that sets <VAR> has that value

column3: 0=60 fps,1=30 fps steady,2=30 fps + frame generation,3=60 fps + frame generation (experimental)
column8: 60 fps is the default (as HookLink 1.5.1 ran). 30 fps + frame generation draws a steady 30 and the screen shows 60, cooler and smoother than 60 fps on most iPhones. 30 fps steady runs coolest. Frame generation draws at that rate and shows twice as many frames (60, or 120 on a 120 Hz screen), with a little more input delay. A mode sets Frame rate, Frame generation and Hold frames when late for you.
Shows 60 frames a second while the game draws 30: MetalFX makes a frame between each two. Less work and heat than 60 fps, with more input delay than real 60; fast motion can smear.
Lets the game lower its resolution under load, which keeps the frame rate up in busy areas. Turn off for a steadier, sharper picture on a fast iPhone.
Less heat, so the phone keeps its speed longer: the 3D picture at 50 % whatever Render scale says, and frame generation's in-between frames at half size. A softer picture.

The title and opening movies skip the game's movie sharpening, which takes about 15 ms of GPU a frame and kept the title screen under 60 fps. A slightly softer movie. Off: the movies as the game makes them.

The lightest the game can run, for older or smaller iPhones and long sessions: the 3D picture at 25 %, frame generation's in-between frames at half size, and memory savers (pipelines warmed into the system's cache instead of kept, shared textures let go sooner). The rows it sets are locked while it's on.
Uses more GPU time and can increase heat.

MetalFX is the default in HookLink: Apple's scaler takes far less GPU time than the game's own network on an iPhone (HookLink issue 3: an iPhone 17 Pro ran 30 fps + frame generation at 14-20 ms of GPU with it)
Fill crops the game's 16:9 picture to cover the screen. Health bars, subtitles or maps near the edges can be cut off. A full-screen picture without cropping needs a patch for each game.
Adds the phone's heat and the battery with the play time it leaves under the frame rate.

Lighter makes the in-between frames at 0.75 of the picture's size, and MetalFX scales the picture back up: about half of frame generation's GPU time, for a slightly softer picture, the HUD too. Recommended: Full; Lighter if frames drop in busy areas.

Finds how the picture moved, so fast camera turns are placed better. Off makes the in-between frames much cheaper (about a third of the GPU time on an iPhone 17 Pro) with softer fast motion: try it if 30 fps + frame generation drops frames.

Lets a game that listens hear you, such as playing the ocarina by humming or whistling the notes. iOS asks for the microphone once; the game's sound then plays through an audio session that also records. Recommended: on to play the ocarina by voice.
The colours of the on-screen controls.
How see-through the on-screen controls are, from 20 % to fully drawn. Takes effect the next time the game starts.
Plays Joy-Con 2 and Pro Controller 2 over Bluetooth: hold Sync on one during the game to pair it. macOS asks once for Bluetooth access.

Fills the whole iPhone screen with a wider 3D view; the HUD, menus and movies stay 16:9 in the middle. Experimental: slower and warmer (about a fifth more pixels). On an unfolded iPhone Duo or an iPad it fills the squarer screen with a taller view instead (not tested yet; the HUD is a little narrow there). Takes effect the next time the game starts.

column7: Wide view: HUD in the middle
column8: Keeps the HUD, menus and movies at their 16:9 shape in the middle of the wider picture. Off spreads them over the whole screen.
Renders about a quarter more pixels: a little slower and warmer.

Objects the game found hidden last frame (behind hills, walls) are not drawn while this frame's answer is on its way. Saves GPU time in Hyrule Field, but in Ocarina of Time it can draw Link, horses and grass in view as pale-blue blocks: the game moves its visibility tests between frames.

On: the game's lower-priority threads may run on the efficiency cores, which keeps the phone cooler. Off (experimental): every game thread competes for the fast cores; hotter, and on some iPhones the GPU then slows down.

Off by default. On keeps the game's model optimizer off the fast cores, but on iPhone it then falls behind and the game draws two to three times as many objects in Hyrule Field (test31 and test32 logs), so leave it off.

column7: Hold 30 fps when the phone is hot
column8: While iOS reports serious heat, the game is held at a steady 30 fps instead of an uneven higher rate. It goes back by itself when the phone cools.

Tells iOS each frame's deadline, so it keeps the game on the fast cores at a higher clock. Uses more power and heat. On a Mac only: on an iPhone 17 Pro it moved the game to the fast cores but the GPU then took 2 to 3 times longer (one power budget), 12-16 fps.
Up to one frame more display latency.
Keeps a pipeline archive; uses more memory.
The first start waits a few minutes for it, once.
